cves.d:
In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a user who does not hold the "admin" or "power" Splunk roles could use the apps backup and restore Representational State Transfer (REST) API to prevent subsequent apps backup or restore operations until Splunk Enterprise restarts. This could result in a Denial of Service (DoS).
The vulnerability is possible because the apps backup and restore REST API handlers do not correctly enforce authorization.
In JetBrains TeamCity before 2026.2.1 stored XSS in the Pull Requests health report for Space connections was possible

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, an unauthenticated user could access RapidDiag process metadata and log file inventory information through the Representational State Transfer (REST) API.
The vulnerability is possible because certain RapidDiag REST API endpoints accept a factory-default shared key for node authentication, which lets requests bypass Splunk user authentication.
For more information see Using RapidDiag (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/troubleshoot/9.0/contact-splunk-support/using-rapiddiag) and Secure Splunk Enterprise services with pass4SymmKey (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.0/secure-distributed-and-clustered-splunk-environments/secure-splunk-enterprise-services-with-pass4symmkey) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, an unauthenticated user could send repeated HTTP PubSub channel subscription requests that cause a Denial of Service (DoS) by permanently increasing memory usage until Splunk Enterprise exhausts available memory. 
The vulnerability affects instances that turn on the [pubsubsvr-http] stanza in server.conf because the HTTP PubSub broker does not release memory associated with a channel after the client disconnects.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, an unauthenticated user with network-path interception capability could cause attacker-controlled JavaScript to run in the browser of a security analyst who previews a Portable Document Format (PDF) attachment in Mission Control. The JavaScript could expose data and perform actions available to the security analyst.
The vulnerability is possible because Mission Control loads the PDF rendering worker from an external content delivery network.
The vulnerability requires the unauthenticated user to intercept the network path to the external content delivery network and a security analyst to preview a PDF attachment in Mission Control. The unauthenticated user should not be able to exploit the vulnerability at will.
For more information see Collaborate on investigations in Splunk Enterprise Security (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/administer/8.7/investigations/collaborate-on-investigations-in-splunk-enterprise-security) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user that holds a role with the edit_modinput_data_migrator capability could cause the data migration input to run arbitrary Search Processing Language (SPL) commands with elevated permissions. With this access, the user could read data outside the assigned role scope and write data to indexes and lookup tables.
The vulnerability is possible because the data migration input does not restrict configured searches to product-supplied migration tasks before it runs them with elevated permissions.
For more information see Capability reference for Splunk Enterprise Security (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/install/8.7/installation/capability-reference-for-splunk-enterprise-security) in the Splunk documentation.

memtomem-stm is a short-term memory proxy gateway with proactive memory surfacing for AI agents. From 0.1.0 until 0.1.34, untrusted long-term and working-memory fields can introduce Markdown or HTML-compatible structure into the surfaced-memory envelope because those fields are not serialized as inert data. A crafted memory can create misleading structural boundaries or visually conceal surfaced content, affecting how a consuming agent interprets the memory context. Ordinary natural-language persuasion remains a residual model-level risk and is outside the structural serialization flaw. This issue is fixed in version 0.1.34.

In Splunk App for Payment Card Industry Compliance versions below 8.7.0, a user who holds the "ess_user" Splunk Enterprise Security role could add attacker-controlled values to lookup data used by the Primary Functions report. If another authenticated user later selects the value in the Primary Function Summary panel, the Splunk App for Payment Card Industry Compliance could run attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) commands using the permissions of the user who selected the value. With this access, the first user could expose or modify data available to the user who selected the value.
The vulnerability is possible because the Primary Functions report does not safely escape report values before including them in drilldown searches.
For more information see Users and roles for Splunk Enterprise Security (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/install/8.7/installation/users-and-roles-for-splunk-enterprise-security) and Reports (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/splunk-app-for-pci-compliance/user-manual/8.7/using-the-splunk-app-for-pci-compliance/reports) in the Splunk documentation.

aMQTT is an open source MQTT broker and client. From 0.11.0 until 0.12.1, the QoS 2 transaction handler in amqtt/mqtt/protocol/handler.py, _handle_qos2_message_flow(), can retain transaction state and packet identifiers when a client disconnects before the handshake completes, unlike QoS 1 flows that expire after the default five-second timeout. A remote client can repeatedly begin QoS 2 flows and disconnect without maintaining long-lived connections; anonymous clients can do this with the default configuration, while authenticated deployments remain affected when a client may initiate QoS 2 flows. The retained state grows broker memory until resource exhaustion can terminate the process; no confidentiality or integrity impact is identified. This issue is fixed in version 0.12.1.

In Splunk Enterprise for Windows versions below 10.4.4, 10.2.8, 10.0.11, and 9.4.16, a user that holds a role with the edit_user capability could create multiple user accounts that share the same user directory. This could expose user-specific configuration between those accounts, let one account modify configuration used by another account, or disrupt features that depend on separate user directories.
The vulnerability is caused by improper validation of usernames before Splunk Enterprise performs Windows filesystem operations. Windows removes trailing periods from directory names, so distinct usernames can resolve to the same user directory.
For more information see Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.6/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.4, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.16, a user who does not hold the "admin" or "power" Splunk roles could use the search jobs Representational State Transfer (REST) API to access indexed events that the srchFilter setting for the role should hide. The same user could also run internal Search Processing Language (SPL) commands and bypass SPL safeguards for risky commands within indexes that the role can search.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk Enterprise does not correctly escape required field values before it includes them in an internally generated search.
For more information, see Search endpoint descriptions (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/rest-api-reference/9.4/search-endpoints/search-endpoint-descriptions), authorize.conf (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/admin-manual/10.4/configuration-file-reference/10.4.5-configuration-file-reference/authorize.conf), and SPL safeguards for risky commands (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.6/best-practices-for-splunk-platform-security/spl-safeguards-for-risky-commands).

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a user who holds the "power" Splunk role could create and share a dashboard that contains attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL). The SPL could run using the permissions of the user who opens the dashboard. With this access, the user who created the dashboard could expose stored credentials and write data to an index.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk Enterprise does not correctly escape field names in searches that use the rename command.
For more information see rename (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/spl-search-reference/10.4/search-commands/rename) and SPL safeguards for risky commands (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.4/best-practices-for-splunk-platform-security/spl-safeguards-for-risky-commands) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user that holds a role with the run_collect capability could store attacker-controlled values in Intrusion Detection data. If another user who can access the Intrusion Search dashboard selects an affected row, Splunk Enterprise Security could run attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) commands using the permissions of the user who selects the row. The user who stores the values could then access sensitive data and modify data available to the user who selects the row.
The vulnerability is possible because the Intrusion Search dashboard encodes data-model field values for the drilldown link but does not escape the values as SPL search literals before inserting the values into drilldown searches.
For more information see Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.4/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities) and Network dashboards (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/user-guide/8.7/analytics/network-dashboards) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user that holds a role with the run_collect capability could store attacker-controlled values in managed-lookup audit data. If another user who can access the Managed Lookups Audit dashboard selects an affected row, Splunk Enterprise Security could run attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) commands using the permissions of the user who selects the row. The user who stores the values could then access sensitive data and modify some data available to the user who selects the row.
The vulnerability is possible because the Managed Lookups Audit dashboard does not safely escape audit data before inserting it into drilldown searches.
For more information see Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.4/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities) and Audit dashboards (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/user-guide/8.7/analytics/audit-dashboards) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, an unauthenticated user who can influence indexed event data could store attacker-controlled values in event fields. If another authenticated user who reviews the event selects the View Adaptive Response Invocations or View Adaptive Response Results workflow action from Event Actions, Splunk Enterprise Security could run attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) commands using the permissions of the user who selects the action. The unauthenticated user could then access or modify sensitive data and disrupt services available to the user who selects the action.
The vulnerability is possible because the affected Common Information Model workflow actions insert the orig_sid and orig_rid event-field values directly into searches without safely validating or quoting the values.
For more information see About workflow actions in Splunk Web (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/manage-knowledge-objects/knowledge-management-manual/10.2/workflow-actions/about-workflow-actions-in-splunk-web) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user with edit permission for containers on only a subset of container labels could modify container pins outside the container labels that the role permits.
The vulnerability is possible because the Container Pin Representational State Transfer (REST) API does not enforce the container label authorization boundary when handling requests.
For more information see Manage roles and permissions in Splunk SOAR (On-premises) (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/administer-soar-on-premises/6.4.1/manage-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-users-and-accounts/manage-roles-and-permissions-in-splunk-soar-on-premises) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user with permission to view and modify containers with an allowed label could add artifacts to containers that the user cannot view or modify.
The vulnerability is possible because the Representational State Transfer (REST) API artifact-creation workflow does not preserve the authorization boundary for the selected container.

In Splunk Enterprise Security versions below 8.7.0, a user that holds a role with the run_collect capability could store attacker-controlled values in intrusion detection data. Another user who holds the "pci_user" role could later select the corresponding row in the Intrusion Detection and Prevention System Alert Activity Details panel. The report could then run attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) commands using the permissions of the user who selected the row. The commands could access data and perform actions available to the user who selected the row.
The vulnerability is possible because the Intrusion Detection and Prevention System Alert Activity report does not treat intrusion detection values as literal search values when it builds the details drilldown search.
For more information see Reports (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/splunk-app-for-pci-compliance/user-manual/8.7/using-the-splunk-app-for-pci-compliance/reports) and Configure users and roles (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise-security-8/splunk-app-for-pci-compliance/installation-and-configuration-manual/8.7/configure-the-app/configure-users-and-roles) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, an authenticated user with permission to view and edit containers for one label could use a slash command through the Representational State Transfer (REST) API to access sensitive product data and credentials outside the authorized container scope.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk SOAR does not enforce authorization for related objects that slash commands access from an authorized artifact.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, an authenticated user that holds a role with the System Settings view permission but not the Assets view permission could view asset and tenant metadata in the ingestion history view.
The ingestion history view does not restrict summary results to assets and tenants that the user can view.

Vulnerability in the Oracle Hyperion Infrastructure Technology product of Oracle Hyperion (component: Installation and Configuration).   The supported version that is affected is 11.2.26.0.000. Easily exploitable vulnerability allows low privileged attacker with network access via HTTP to compromise Oracle Hyperion Infrastructure Technology.  Successful attacks require human interaction from a person other than the attacker and while the vulnerability is in Oracle Hyperion Infrastructure Technology, attacks may significantly impact additional products (scope change). Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in  unauthorized access to critical data or complete access to all Oracle Hyperion Infrastructure Technology accessible data as well as  unauthorized update, insert or delete access to some of Oracle Hyperion Infrastructure Technology accessible data. CVSS 3.1 Base Score 7.6 (Confidentiality and Integrity impacts).  CVSS Vector: (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:L/A:N).

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user with asset edit permission could change the approval requirements and effective automation user for an asset without Splunk SOAR recording field-level audit details for those changes. This could weaken investigation and accountability for changes to security-sensitive asset settings.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk SOAR does not include the asset approval voting fields and effective automation user field in its field-level audit coverage.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user with permission to author and run playbooks could add messages to a different playbook run log and cause that run to fail, including runs outside the labels that the user could access.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk SOAR does not verify that playbook API requests use the trusted runtime context for the current playbook run.

In Splunk App for Stream versions below 8.1.7, an unauthenticated user could cause Splunk App for Stream to reset its in-memory indexer cache.
The vulnerability exists because the Splunk Web handler accepts the cache-reset request without requiring a login.
For more information see Splunk Stream installation package overview (https://help.splunk.com/en/data-management/collect-stream-data/install-and-configure-splunk-stream/8.0/introduction/splunk-stream-installation-package-overview) and Launch Splunk Web (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/admin-manual/10.6/administer-splunk-enterprise-with-splunk-web/launch-splunk-web) in the Splunk documentation.

Vulnerability in the Oracle Hyperion Planning product of Oracle Hyperion (component: Security).   The supported version that is affected is 11.2.26.0.000. Difficult to exploit vulnerability allows unauthenticated attacker with network access via Oracle Net to compromise Oracle Hyperion Planning.  Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in  unauthorized creation, deletion or modification access to critical data or all Oracle Hyperion Planning accessible data as well as  unauthorized access to critical data or complete access to all Oracle Hyperion Planning accessible data. CVSS 3.1 Base Score 7.4 (Confidentiality and Integrity impacts).  CVSS Vector: (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N).

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user that holds a role with the System Settings edit permission could cause Splunk SOAR to send a stored Elasticsearch password to a host that the user controls.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk SOAR reuses a stored Elasticsearch password for a changed Search Settings endpoint without requiring a replacement password.

ALTCHA is a Go library for creating and verifying ALTCHA challenges. Prior to 2.1.0, parseServerSignature can leave ServerSignatureVerificationData.Extra uninitialized when url.ParseQuery returns partial values and an error for a malformed percent escape in VerificationData. A later write of an unknown parsed key to the nil map panics before VerifyServerSignature or VerifyServerSignatureSafe completes signature verification, so an unauthenticated client can abort a request. Standard net/http recovers the request goroutine, while application goroutines or frameworks without recovery can crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 2.1.0.
In JetBrains TeamCity before 2026.2.1, 2026.1.5 stored XSS in the Commit Status Publisher settings was possible

CKAN is an open-source data management system for data hubs and data portals. Prior to 2.10.11 and 2.11.6, the web user registration flow authenticates a newly registered account without first regenerating the session identifier when server-side session storage is configured. An attacker who can set a session cookie in a victim's browser or obtain the victim's current valid session identifier can reuse that identifier after the victim registers, gaining access to the new account. CKAN uses cookie-based sessions by default, and web registration is disabled by default through ckan.auth.create_user_via_web. This issue is fixed in CKAN 2.10.11, 2.11.6, and 2.12.0.
In JetBrains TeamCity before 2026.2.1 stored XSS in the Amazon EC2 cloud profile editor was possible

Iceburg CRM through 5.0.0 contains an incorrect authorization vulnerability in Module::saveRecord() that allows authenticated users to write to unauthorized modules by prefixing request body keys with another module id. Attackers with write access to one module can submit crafted requests to POST /data/save or PUT /api/crm/{id} to set their role_id to Admin and access administrative data.

Bar Assistant 3.0.0 before 6.11.0 contains an authorization bypass vulnerability in BarController::join that allows authenticated users to join bars without a valid invite code. Attackers can send POST requests to /api/bars/join omitting invite_code, matching invite-disabled bars with NULL codes, to read cocktails, ingredients, members, settings and search tokens.
In JetBrains TeamCity before 2026.2.1 missing authorization allowed reading VCS file contents and patches of other projects

Budibase is an open-source low-code platform. Prior to 3.50.0, the public POST /api/global/users/init endpoint on a self-hosted single-tenant deployment accepts an attacker-controlled tenantId and evaluates checkAnyUserExists() in the selected tenant database instead of the legitimate default tenant. An unauthenticated attacker can select an unused tenant namespace to bypass the one-time initialization guard, causing packages/worker/src/api/controllers/global/users.ts to create a tenant-specific CouchDB database and a global-administrator document without a session or CSRF token. Repeating this operation with unique tenant identifiers can exhaust datastore resources and leave latent privileged records. The created administrator cannot log into the default tenant while multi-tenancy remains disabled, which limits the immediate impact to persistent writes, denial of service, and records that may become usable during later multi-tenant operation or migration. This issue is fixed in versions 3.50.0 and 4.0.0.
In JetBrains TeamCity before 2026.2.1 stored XSS in VMware vSphere cloud profile settings was possible

Flyto2 Core is an execution kernel for automation and AI-agent workflows. Prior to 2.26.8, validate_url_ssrf in src/core/utils.py resolves and checks a hostname but returns the hostname URL rather than the validated address, and session.get in http.get performs an independent DNS lookup when connecting. A low-privileged caller with control of the hostname's DNS can make the first lookup return a public address and the connection-time lookup return an internal address, bypassing the SSRF guard for all modules that call it and exposing readable internal or metadata-service responses. Successful exploitation requires attacker-controlled DNS and a successful timing-dependent answer change between the two lookups. This issue is fixed in version 2.26.8.

netty-incubator-codec-ohttp implements Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP) gateway and client functionality using Netty. From 0.0.20.Final until 0.0.27.Final, OHttpClientCodec in codec-ohttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpClientCodec.java and OHttpServerCodec in codec-ohttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpServerCodec.java retain the consumed outer cumulationBuffer after a valid OHTTP exchange completes, even though OHttpRequestResponseContext.destroy in codec-ohttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpRequestResponseContext.java releases the inner Binary HTTP cumulation and the channel remains active. A peer can complete a large request or response and leave the keep-alive connection idle, causing the client and server handlers to retain the current high-water pooled or direct buffer capacity until later inbound content replaces it or the handler is removed. Many long-lived idle connections can pin substantial memory and create availability pressure. The issue does not cause unbounded growth for repeated exchanges on a single channel. This issue is fixed in version 0.0.27.Final.

netty-incubator-codec-ohttp implements Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP) gateway and client functionality using Netty. Prior to 0.0.23.Final, BinaryHttpParser in codec-bhttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/bhttp/BinaryHttpParser.java accumulates attacker-controlled Binary HTTP variable-length integers into the int offset sumBytes. BinaryHttpParser.readRequestHead, BinaryHttpParser.readFieldLine, and BinaryHttpParser.getIndeterminateLength can narrow long lengths into that offset, causing integer wraparound before buffer indices are calculated. A remote peer that supplies a valid large encoded length to BinaryHttpParser or BinaryHttpDecoder can trigger an unchecked bounds exception from a small malformed message, fail or close the channel, and repeatedly cause denial of service. Java and Netty bounds checks prevent memory corruption, and no information disclosure was observed. This issue is fixed in version 0.0.23.Final.

A weakness has been identified in OSGeo shapelib up to 1.6.3. This vulnerability affects the function DBFCloneEmpty of the file dbfopen.c. This manipulation causes null pointer dereference. It is possible to launch the attack on the local host. Patch name: f79050a900d2a05529501b2b714b8f89067db071. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue.

StorageGRID (formerly StorageGRID Webscale) versions 12.1.0 and higher are susceptible to an information exposure vulnerability which allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to acquire low-sensitivity credentials via a Man-in-the-middle attack when certain non-default features are enabled.

The Canva Desktop App before 1.128.0 stores encrypted application state on disk. The encryption key is hardcoded as a plaintext string in the main.js file and is identical across all Canva installations on Windows and macOS.

NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM for any platform contains a vulnerability where a user may cause a race condition by running concurrent requests. A successful exploit of this vulnerability may lead to data tampering.

Multiple products produced by Ruijie Networks Co., Ltd. contain an OS command injection vulnerability that may lead to arbitrary OS commands being executed by an attacker with the administrative privilege.

A flaw was found in Keycloak. When processing token requests using the User-Managed Access (UMA) grant, Keycloak fails to verify whether a target client or resource server is enabled before issuing an authorization token. An authenticated remote user can exploit this flaw to obtain valid Requesting Party Tokens (RPTs) for disabled clients, bypassing administrative access controls and permissions restrictions.

Flowintel , contained a session management vulnerability in its browser authentication mechanism. The session identifier used a bare numeric user ID rather than a credential-bound token, resulting in several related weaknesses:

- Remembered logins (remember-me cookies) remained valid after a user changed their password, allowing an attacker holding a previously issued cookie to retain access indefinitely.
- Server-side session identifiers were not rotated upon login (local, SSO, or remembered), enabling session fixation.
- Self-service email and password changes did not require verification of the current password, permitting an attacker with an active session to modify account credentials without knowledge of the existing password.
- Administrator-initiated password resets did not revoke other browser sessions, invalidate remembered logins, or rotate the affected user's API key.

An attacker who obtained a valid session or remember-me cookie (e.g., through XSS, network interception, or cookie theft) could maintain unauthorized access even after the legitimate user changed their password. Additionally, an attacker with any valid session could change the account's email address or password without knowing the current credentials, effectively taking over the account.

Affected versions: Flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

The
Danfoss legacy AK-SC 355 and AK-SM 800 Series are vulnerable to unauthorized
access when default credentials or known passwords are used for authentication.
These products were manufactured with default credentials documented in the
product manual. All versions are affected.

Flowintel contains a privilege escalation vulnerability in its Matrix relay (bot) integration. When the relay forwarded API requests on behalf of a represented user, the authorization and permission checks evaluated the relay bot's elevated role while the request handlers acted as the lower-privileged represented user. This mismatch allowed users with restricted roles (e.g., Read Only) to perform write operations, directory lookups, calendar modifications, assignment changes, template creation, and import actions they were not authorized to perform.

Additionally, relay authority was determined by matching editable user profile fields (name and email) rather than a protected, non-spoofable identifier. An ordinary user who modified their profile to match the expected bot name could be recognized as the trusted relay, enabling impersonation of the bot and potential access to its elevated privileges.

Preconditions:
- A valid Flowintel user account with a restricted role (e.g., Read Only)
- Access to the Matrix relay integration or the ability to send API requests with the relay's API key and a MATRIX-ID header
- For the impersonation vector: ability to edit one's own profile name fields

Security impact:
- Unauthorized write operations by users with read-only or otherwise restricted permissions
- Potential impersonation of the trusted relay bot by ordinary users
- Bypass of organization-level access controls and role-based restrictions
- Unauthorized modification of cases, tasks, calendar events, templates, and user directory entries

Affected versions: Flowintel prior to 4.1.0

Flowintel contains multiple SSO identity and organisation trust boundary violations that collectively allow account takeover, privilege escalation, and unauthorized access to private case data.

- Keycloak SSO accepted unverified email claims, and all SSO providers (Keycloak, Entra ID, SimpleSAML) could resolve a claimed email address to an existing account that was created via a different sign-in method, enabling cross-provider account collision and unauthorized access to another user's account and data.

- Entra ID role mapping relied on group display names, which tenant members could duplicate by creating a group with the same name as a privileged group (e.g. FlowintelAdmin), resulting in unauthorized role escalation.

- SSO provisioning reused organisations whose display names matched user-controlled profile names, granting the new SSO user access to that organisation's private cases without explicit administrator assignment.

- Case sharing via the API resolved organisations by name using a first-match query, so ambiguous names could silently resolve to the wrong organisation.

Preconditions: an attacker must have a valid SSO identity (Keycloak, Entra ID, or SimpleSAML) or be a member of the relevant Entra tenant. No local administrator access is required.

Security impact: unauthorized access to private case data, privilege escalation to Editor or higher roles, and account takeover across authentication providers.

Affected versions: Flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

Authorization omission in the 'admusers' operation of the POST request to '/xmanagercore/api/services/' in XOneManager 3.8.3.0. The API fails to verify the required role for querying the directory. An authenticated member of the project can obtain the list of platform accounts—including administrative accounts—along with details such as email addresses, roles, and associated companies.

FlowIntel contains an authorization bypass in its user directory and assignment endpoints that allows authenticated users to access data belonging to other organisations.

When the LIMIT_USER_VIEW_TO_ORG setting is enabled to restrict directory visibility to the caller's organisation, several API endpoints (user lookup by ID, last name, Matrix ID, and role-based listings) did not consistently enforce the organisation boundary. An authenticated non-admin user could retrieve profiles of users in other organisations by supplying their identifiers.

Additionally, OrgAdmin users could retrieve the task assignments of any user in the system, including tasks and case titles from private cases to which they had no access. The assignment endpoints did not verify that the requested user belonged to the caller's organisation or that the underlying cases were visible to the caller.

Security impact:
- Exposure of user identities (names, Matrix IDs, roles) across organisation boundaries
- Disclosure of task assignments, case titles, and workflow details from private cases
- Potential enumeration of other organisations' membership and case activity

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0

FlowIntel contains multiple authorization and credential management vulnerabilities affecting connector instances, MISP helper tools, and case templates.

- Connector instance metadata, connectivity checks, and case listings accepted instance IDs without verifying if the acting user had visibility or ownership rights, allowing unauthorized access to sensitive configuration and data.
- Case template serialization and creation processes exposed connector instances attached to templates regardless of the user's permissions, potentially leaking credentials or instance details to users who should not have access.
- Editing connector instances allowed changes to URLs or sharing scopes without requiring re-authentication of API keys, enabling the reuse of another user's credentials in a new context or the leakage of shared keys to unauthorized endpoints.
- Outbound MISP connector keys were incorrectly accepted for authenticating incoming alerts, bypassing the intended separation between outbound integration credentials and inbound alert source authentication.

These issues allow authenticated users to access unauthorized connector data, manipulate credential scopes, and potentially exploit credential confusion between different security contexts.

Affected versions: < 4.1.0

flowintel contains multiple authorization bypass vulnerabilities in its Analyzer (MISP Modules) functionality, affecting both the web interface and the REST API.

- Saving analyzer results to a case or task accepted caller-supplied case and task identifiers without verifying that the authenticated user is a member of the target case or holds the required restricted-task permissions. An authenticated user could write notes, create tasks, and attach MISP objects or attributes into another organization's case.

- Stored analyzer results were retrievable by UUID by any authenticated user. Both the web endpoint and the API endpoint returned the full result payload without checking ownership, exposing another user's analysis output.

- The save handler did not validate the structure of the request, did not reject conflicting destination selections, and did not halt processing when a task-note operation failed, allowing partial or unintended writes.

Preconditions: the attacker must possess a valid authenticated session (or API token) in flowintel. No administrative role is required.

Security impact: unauthorized cross-tenant data disclosure (analyzer results) and unauthorized cross-tenant data modification (notes, tasks, MISP objects/attributes in another organization's case).

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

cves.d:
flowintel contains an authorization bypass in its task completion workflow for privileged cases. Users with lower-privilege roles (editor, queuer) were able to mark tasks as completed without the required approver review (Admin, Case Admin, or Queue Admin), undermining the approval workflow.

The vulnerability was exploitable through multiple paths:
- Direct task completion via browser UI or REST API
- Changing a task's status to "Finished", which implicitly completed the task
- Creating a new task in a privileged case with the completed flag already set
- Using UUID aliases or Matrix delegation to reach the same endpoints

Preconditions:
- An authenticated user with at least editor or queuer role
- A privileged case with tasks in a non-completed state

Security impact:
- Bypass of the mandatory approver review process for privileged cases
- Unauthorized modification of task completion state
- Potential to mark sensitive work as finished without proper oversight

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0

FlowIntel contains an authorization bypass that allows non-approver case members to modify restricted tasks (those in Requested, Rejected, or Request Review status) through several indirect code paths that lacked the required approver permission check.

Affected operations include:
- Self-unassignment from a restricted task
- Reordering tasks, including indirectly moving restricted sibling tasks
- Linking or unlinking MISP objects and attributes to/from restricted tasks
- Creating MISP objects or standalone attributes with task IDs referencing restricted tasks
- Deleting MISP objects or attributes that are linked to restricted tasks
- Executing modules on restricted tasks

A user with case member access (but without Admin, Case Admin, or Queue Admin privileges) could exploit these paths to alter the state of tasks that are supposed to be locked pending approval, effectively bypassing the intended approval workflow and potentially manipulating associated MISP data.

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0

FlowIntel contains a missing authorization vulnerability in its task file deletion functionality. When a privileged task is in a restricted state (Requested, Rejected, or Request Review), any authenticated user with basic case membership (e.g., editor or queuer) was able to delete evidence files associated with that task via both the browser interface and the REST API. The deletion operation should have been restricted to users holding Admin, Case Admin, or Queue Admin roles.

The vulnerability affects the core file deletion logic, the browser-facing task endpoint, and the API task endpoint. No role-based restriction was enforced prior to performing disk removal, database record deletion, timeline event removal, or history log updates.

An attacker with a low-privilege case membership could destroy evidence files, corrupt investigation timelines, and alter case history, compromising the integrity of ongoing investigations.

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0.

flowintel contains an authorization bypass in the file-to-note conversion feature for case tasks. When a task is in a restricted workflow state (Requested, Rejected, or Request Review) within a privileged case, the conversion endpoint did not enforce elevated role requirements. Any authenticated user with basic case membership (e.g., editor or queuer) could invoke the conversion action, causing the system to read the attached file contents and create a note on the restricted task.

This bypasses the intended workflow restriction that only Admin, Case Admin, or Queue Admin roles may modify tasks in those states. An attacker with a low-privilege account in a privileged case could:
- Extract file contents into note format, potentially circumventing file-level access controls
- Create unauthorized notes that alter the task's note count, modification timestamp, and case history
- Disrupt the review/approval workflow on restricted tasks

The vulnerability requires an authenticated user with at least editor-level access to the affected case and a task in one of the restricted states.

Affected versions: flowintel < 4.1.0

FlowIntel contains an authorization bypass in its case serialization logic that allows an authenticated user to view metadata of private cases they do not have access to.

When a case is linked to another case, the JSON representation of the source case included the ID, title, and description of every linked case regardless of the requesting user's permissions. This affected multiple access paths:

- Browser views (case detail, case info, search, calendar)
- REST API endpoints (get case, list cases, search, title lookup, completed/not-completed lists)
- Internal tooling and connector module context building

An attacker with valid credentials and access to any case that contains a link to a private case could enumerate the private case's identifier, title, and description without holding a membership or role on that private case. The exposure occurred because the serialization method did not receive or evaluate the acting user's identity before including linked-case data in the response.

Security impact:
- Disclosure of private case identifiers, titles, and descriptions to unauthorized users
- Facilitation of further targeted attacks against the exposed private cases
- Bypass of the intended per-case access control model

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0

flowintel contains a vulnerability in the MISP correlation feature that allows unauthorized disclosure of case identifiers.

The application failed to enforce proper access controls when generating correlation lists for MISP attributes. Specifically, the system did not verify whether the requesting user had permission to view the source case or the matching cases returned in the correlation results. This lack of authorization checks allowed authenticated users to potentially discover the existence of cases they do not have access to, leading to information disclosure.

The vulnerability affects the following components:
- Case correlation logic
- API endpoints for retrieving correlation attributes
- MISP object handling

Affected versions: < 4.1.0

FlowIntel, a threat intelligence case management platform, contains an information disclosure vulnerability in its case serialization logic. When a case is rendered via the REST API or browser views, all connector instances associated with that case were included in the response regardless of the requesting user's permissions.

This means that any authenticated user with read access to a case could observe connector metadata belonging to other users (personal-scope connectors) or other organizations (org-scope connectors), including connector URLs, descriptions, UUIDs, and potentially embedded API credentials.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated user account with at least read access to the affected case
- The case must have connector instances attached that belong to other users or organizations

Impact:
- Disclosure of personal connector endpoints and credentials of other users
- Disclosure of organization-scoped connector metadata across organizational boundaries
- Enumeration of connector infrastructure (URLs, UUIDs, descriptions) not intended for the viewer

Affected versions: < 4.1.0

FlowIntel contains an authorization bypass in its task management workflow. When a user reopens a completed task (by toggling its completion state or changing its status to a non-finished value) or creates a new task within a completed privileged case, the parent case is automatically revived (un-completed, status reset to Created, finish date cleared). The system failed to enforce the required Admin or Case Admin privilege check before performing this case revival side effect.

A user with basic task-level permissions (e.g., editor, queuer, or queue admin) could trigger the revival of a completed privileged case through the browser interface or the REST API, without holding the elevated role required for case-level operations. This could disrupt case lifecycle management, clear completion metadata, and potentially expose the case to further unauthorized modifications.

The vulnerability affects both the browser-based task completion/status-change endpoints and the corresponding API endpoints, as well as the task creation flow.

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0.

flowintel contains an authorization bypass in the browser-based admin user editing interface. The edit_user view in the admin panel verified that a non-platform-admin user could only edit accounts belonging to their own organization, but it did not verify that the target account was not a platform-admin account. As a result, an authenticated user holding an organization-admin role could open the edit form for any platform-admin account and submit modifications, including changes to credentials, roles, or other account attributes.

The API layer already enforced a restriction preventing non-admin users from targeting admin accounts, but the browser-based admin view lacked the equivalent check, creating an inconsistent authorization boundary.

Impact:
- Unauthorized modification of platform-admin account data (integrity)
- Potential lockout or privilege manipulation of platform administrators (availability)
- Escalation of an organization-admin role to effectively control platform-level administration

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

A vulnerability exists in the flowintel application's calendar functionality that allows unauthorized access to private case data. The task calendar queries failed to enforce visibility checks on the parent case associated with tasks. Specifically, tasks assigned to a user or belonging to the user's organization were returned in calendar views (including browser and API ICS feeds) without verifying whether the user had permission to view the parent case. This allowed users to potentially discover and access details of private cases they were not authorized to view, leading to information disclosure.

The issue affected the default task visibility logic and the assigned-only task queries. The fix ensures that case visibility is rechecked in addition to task assignment or organization membership, preventing the exposure of private case data in calendar outputs.

Affected versions: flowintel < 4.1.0

flowintel contains an authorization flaw in its recurring reminder notification subsystem. When a user is subscribed to recurring notifications for a case, the system does not re-verify the recipient's current access rights to that case before generating or displaying the notification.

As a result, a user who previously had access to a private case and later had that access revoked can still:
- Receive recurring reminder notifications containing case-related content.
- View stored reminder notifications in their notification list, including notification counts, even though they no longer have permission to view the underlying case.

The vulnerability affects both the notification creation path (recurring reminder generation) and the notification display path (listing and counting stored reminders). The issue arises because the authorization check performed at subscription time is not re-applied at delivery or retrieval time.

Security impact is limited to information disclosure: an unauthorized user may observe case titles, reminder messages, and associated metadata that they no longer have permission to access. No integrity or availability impact is indicated by the patch.

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

FlowIntel's alerting module contained an authorization bypass in the alert access control logic. When an alert was linked to a private case, the system relied solely on connector ownership (user or organization) to determine access, without verifying that the requesting user still held valid membership in the associated private case.

This meant that a user who was a connector owner of an alert could continue to read alert details, review history, raw payloads, and action comments, and could perform review-status updates or case-creation actions, even after their access to the linked private case had been revoked or they were never a member of that case.

Additionally, a time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) gap existed: after a review-status update or a competing case-creation claim was committed, the response could disclose private case identifiers or review history to a user whose access had been concurrently removed by another session linking the alert to a private case.

Impact:
- Unauthorized disclosure of private case data (review comments, raw payloads, action history) through alert endpoints.
- Unauthorized modification of alert review status and creation of cases from alerts the user should no longer access.
- Leakage of a competing case identifier to an unauthorized user during concurrent case-creation races.

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0.

flowintel is a case management application that enforces an approval workflow for tasks in privileged cases. Tasks in such cases are required to start in a Requested status, meaning they must receive explicit approval before becoming active.

A logic flaw in the task-creation path allowed tasks to be initialized with a Created status (bypassing the approval step) in two scenarios:

- When a task was created from a template and no acting user was supplied, the privileged-case check was skipped entirely, leaving the task in Created status.
- When a case was created from a template, all copied tasks were unconditionally assigned the Created status regardless of the case's privileged designation.

An authenticated user with the ability to create tasks from templates or to instantiate cases from templates could therefore place tasks directly into an active state within privileged cases, circumventing the intended approval gate. This may expose restricted case content or permit actions that should require supervisory sign-off.

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

Poste.io is vulnerable to remote code execution in DMARC report processing. Email sent to dmarc-reports@<domain> is saved without sender verification. Script that runs as root unpacks the attachments using unsafe shell commands, allowing command injection through crafted attachments (e.g. file names or archive contents). A remote unauthenticated attacker who can send an email to the server's port 25 can execute arbitrary commands as root within the Poste.io container.


This issue was fixed in version 2.5.22.

FlowIntel's chatbot component used a single shared MCP (Model Context Protocol) session and process-wide environment variable to pass per-user API credentials to a child process. Because the session and the ambient FLOWINTEL_API_KEY environment variable were shared across all concurrent requests, a user's authenticated identity could be applied to another user's tool invocation, or a stale/ambient credential could be inherited by a new request.

Preconditions:
- An authenticated user with access to the chatbot interface.
- Concurrent or overlapping chatbot tool invocations from different users, or a request made after another user's credentials were written to the process environment.

Impact:
- A lower-privilege user could read data belonging to a higher-privilege user (e.g., private investigation cases).
- A user whose session was invalidated (deleted, password changed, key revoked) could still operate under a previously cached ambient credential.
- The parent process environment was mutated with user-specific secrets, creating a persistent credential leak surface.

Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0.

flowintel contains a vulnerability in the case and task classification usage endpoints that allows authenticated users to view classification data associated with cases they do not have permission to access.

The affected endpoints, which provide lists of used taxonomies, tags, galaxies, clusters, and custom tags, did not properly enforce object-level access controls. While the endpoints required authentication, they failed to filter the returned data based on the requesting user's visibility permissions for the underlying cases. This allowed any authenticated user to enumerate classification usage across all cases, including private or restricted cases belonging to other organizations or users.

This issue could lead to the disclosure of sensitive information, such as the existence of specific cases, the types of threats or indicators associated with them, and the relationships between different classification elements, potentially aiding an attacker in reconnaissance or targeting.

Affected versions: < 4.1.0

flowintel contains an information disclosure vulnerability in its case history feature. When a user views the history of a case they are authorized to access, the history output includes references to other cases (linked, unlinked, or forked) without verifying whether the requesting user has permission to view those referenced cases. This exposes the identifiers and titles of cases that the user should not be able to discover.

The vulnerability affects multiple output paths:
- Browser-based case history view
- API history endpoint
- Plain-text history download
- Markdown history download
- Report timeline generation

An authenticated user with access to any single case can enumerate the existence and identifiers of other cases by reading the history of a case they can access. This bypasses the intended per-case access control model and may reveal the existence of sensitive investigations, their identifiers, and associated metadata to unauthorized users.

The raw audit storage is not modified; the issue is solely in the presentation layer failing to filter references to inaccessible cases before returning history data to the user.

Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0.

In Postgres Enterprise Manager (PEM), the pem_agent role, which every PEM agent login inherits, is a member of the PostgreSQL pg_read_server_files and pg_write_server_files roles on the PEM backend database. An attacker who controls any monitored host, and so its PEM agent certificate, can read and write files on the PEM server host as the postgres operating system user. This includes the PEM certificate authority key, which lets the attacker issue certificates for other agents and act as them.
From PEM 10.6.1, PEM agents no longer hold these roles.

In Postgres Enterprise Manager (PEM), the row-level security policies on pem.job and pem.jobstep that apply to PEM agents do not limit an agent to its own jobs. An attacker who controls one monitored host, and so its PEM agent certificate, can create, change or delete jobs for every other agent, including the agent on the PEM server. Agents run SQL job steps with the database credentials of the server they monitor, and shell job steps where batch jobs are enabled, so compromising one monitored host can give superuser SQL access to every monitored database and to the PEM backend.
From PEM 10.6.1, PEM agents can no longer create jobs or change job definitions or job steps.

In Postgres Enterprise Manager (PEM), several SECURITY DEFINER functions in the pem schema of the PEM backend database are owned by a superuser but do not set a safe search_path. Any PEM user who can connect to the PEM backend database can create objects that these functions use in place of the intended ones, and so run arbitrary SQL with superuser privileges. Temporary objects can be used for this on every supported PostgreSQL version, and objects in the public schema on PostgreSQL 14 backends and backends upgraded from PostgreSQL 14.
From PEM 10.6.1, these functions run with a fixed search_path.

In Postgres Enterprise Manager (PEM), multi-factor authentication (MFA) is not enforced on the PEM web application's own routes. An attacker who knows the password of a user who has enrolled a second factor can skip the second factor and call PEM's pages and APIs directly, with that user's permissions. A similar issue in pgAdmin 4 was assigned CVE-2024-4215.
From PEM 10.6.1, every authenticated PEM route requires a completed MFA check.

Insertion of Sensitive Information Into Sent Data vulnerability in WP Swings PDF Generator for WordPress pdf-generator-for-wp allows Retrieve Embedded Sensitive Data.This issue affects PDF Generator for WordPress: from n/a through 1.6.5.

In Postgres Enterprise Manager (PEM), the SQL Profiler save and load functions in the PEM web application do not keep the client-supplied file name inside the user's storage directory. A user with the SQL Profiler role (pem_comp_sqlprofiler) can read JSON files, and overwrite files that the PEM web server account can write, outside their own storage directory. Overwriting the PEM web application's configuration database stops the web console for all users.
From PEM 10.6.1, the SQL Profiler only reads and writes files inside the user's storage directory.

In Postgres Enterprise Manager (PEM), webhook URLs are not validated, and the PEM agent does not restrict the URL schemes it uses to deliver webhooks. A user with the alert configuration role (pem_config_alert) can set up a webhook with a file:// URL. When the webhook is sent, the agent on the PEM server, which runs as root by default, reads the local file and stores its contents in the webhook error record in the PEM database, where any PEM user can read it.
From PEM 10.6.1, PEM accepts and sends only http and https webhook URLs.

A weakness has been identified in D-Link DIR-600L 2.17b02. Affected by this issue is some unknown functionality of the file hedwig.cgi of the component fatlady Handler. Executing a manipulation can lead to path traversal. The attack may be launched remotely.

In Postgres Enterprise Manager (PEM), any PEM user can read the encrypted passwords that PEM agents use to connect to monitored servers, including the PEM backend superuser password stored when the PEM server is configured. Unless a custom encryption key is configured, these passwords are encrypted with a key that is the same in every PEM installation, so they can be decrypted.
From PEM 10.6.1, PEM users can no longer read these passwords.

In Postgres Enterprise Manager (PEM), the pem.deploy_job_template() function does not check that the caller can access the servers, groups and agents it deploys a job template to. When PEM teams are used to separate access, a user with the scheduled tasks role (pem_manage_schedule_task) can deploy and schedule SQL or shell job steps on agents that belong to other teams.
From PEM 10.6.1, PEM checks team access for every server, group and agent a template is deployed to.

In Postgres Enterprise Manager (PEM), any PEM user can run the pem.send_webhook() function, which runs with elevated privileges and queues a payload for any configured webhook. The PEM agent then delivers it with that webhook's stored headers, OAuth token or client certificate, so a user can send forged notifications to endpoints they could not otherwise authenticate to.
From PEM 10.6.1, no PEM login role can call this function directly. PEM still sends webhook notifications through its own internal paths.

A vulnerability was detected in declare-lab tango up to 34ecd38898508017ca937508a047b42817d2b070. Impacted is the function Tango.__init__ of the file tango.py of the component Model Loading. Performing a manipulation of the argument scheduler_name results in improper input validation. The attack is possible to be carried out remotely. The exploit is now public and may be used. This product adopts a rolling release strategy to maintain continuous delivery. Therefore, version details for affected or updated releases cannot be specified. The project was informed of the problem early through an issue report but has not responded yet.

A vulnerability was identified in hasan-py Hayroo up to fd0fbe763153f72bfaa04ed1e1e4a1bb6f7c61df. Affected by this issue is the function Product.deleteImages of the file server/controller/products.js of the component Image Deletion Handler. The manipulation leads to path traversal. The attack may be initiated remotely. The exploit is publicly available and might be used. This product uses a rolling release model to deliver continuous updates. As a result, specific version information for affected or updated releases is not available. The identifier of the patch is 9714947bb43ec8559287aa3962b70a7be8c8d6b1. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue.

A flaw was found in Keycloak. When evaluating access permissions, Keycloak Authorization Services improperly matches resource paths containing wildcard file extensions by evaluating only the file extension suffix and ignoring configured path prefixes. An authenticated remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability by requesting a restricted resource that shares a file extension with a more permissive resource, leading to an authorization bypass and unintended access to protected data.

A vulnerability was detected in WebKul QloApps up to 1.8.0. Affected by this vulnerability is the function postProcessDownload/installTheme of the file controllers/admin/AdminModulesController.php of the component Archive Import. The manipulation results in path traversal. It is possible to launch the attack remotely. The exploit is now public and may be used. The vendor was contacted early about this disclosure but did not respond in any way.

Vulnerability in the Oracle Hyperion Planning product of Oracle Hyperion (component: Application Development Framework).   The supported version that is affected is 11.2.26.0.000. Easily exploitable vulnerability allows low privileged attacker with network access via HTTP to compromise Oracle Hyperion Planning. The exploit has been made available to the public and could be used for attacks. This product does not use versioning. This is why information about affected and unaffected releases are unavailable. The project was informed of the problem early through an issue report but has not responded yet.

The VidShop for WooCommerce plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Sensitive Information Exposure in versions up to, and including, 1.10.0 via the /vsfw/v1/products/{id} REST API endpoint. This is due to the endpoint's permission_callback (check_public_permission) returning true unconditionally and the get_item() handler only checking that the product and video exist — it does not check the product's post_status or catalog visibility, nor does it verify that the product is actually linked to the supplied video_id. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to enumerate product IDs and read private, draft, and catalog-hidden WooCommerce products' names, short descriptions, prices, variations, attributes, and stock information that would otherwise be hidden from public view.

The Nelio Content – Editorial Calendar & Social Media Auto-Posting plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to authorization bypass in all versions up to, and including, 5.0.1. This is due to the plugin not properly verifying that a user is authorized to perform an action. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with contributor-level access and above, to view the titles, publication dates, author display names, and author email addresses (including those of administrators) of private, draft, and pending posts they cannot access, and to write arbitrary _nc_url metadata onto posts they cannot edit.

The Charitable – Donation & Fundraising Platform (Donation Forms, Recurring Donations & Fundraising Campaigns) plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'stripe_payment_method' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 1.8.15.1 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. The TeX payload survives WordPress core comment kses intact because it contains no HTML tags, and MathJax is active on fresh installs by default due to the 'chatbot_chatgpt_enable_mathjax' option defaulting to 'Yes' with no page or shortcode presence guard on enqueue.

Improper following of a certificate’s chain of trust in the remote-attestation verifier used to establish trust with Meta AI's confidential computing backend in WhatsApp for iOS before 2.26.24.72, WhatsApp Business for iOS and WhatsApp for Mac Desktop before v2.26.23.72, WhatsApp for Android before v2.26.23.74, and WhatsApp Business for Android before v2.26.23.70 could have allowed someone positioned within Meta infrastructure to bypass the hardware root of trust by presenting clients with a VCEK certificate signed by a key other than the hardware manufacturer’s. Any such VCEK Cert would first have to be published to the third-party binary transparency ledger used by WhatsApp Private Processing. The ledger shows that every published VCEK certificate chains to the hardware root of trust, confirming no exploitation.

A SQL injection vulnerability when the recipient tapped on a specially crafted “order details” message from an unofficial client in WhatsApp for Android prior to version 2.26.35.74 could have allowed deletion of locally-stored WhatsApp files and, only if the user is online at time of receipt, leaked one bit of information asked by the attacker about the user’s chat database via an induced-crash delivery receipt timing sidechannel. We have not seen evidence of exploitation in the wild.

Authenticated UEs repeatedly establishing PDU sessions during NRF or AMF failures leak SM contexts, UE IP addresses and TEIDs, exhausting the DNN IP pool.

Open5GS AMF through 2.8.0 contains a resource leak vulnerability that allows authenticated UEs to exhaust the session pool by triggering failed DNN or S-NSSAI validation. Attackers can repeat PDU Session Establishment Requests with different PDU Session Identity values, leaving stale amf_sess contexts that degrade service for other subscribers.

C-Blosc2 before 3.4.1 contains a heap-based out-of-bounds read vulnerability in frame_decompress_chunk() because sparse frame chunk cbytes are not checked against the actual chunk file size. Attackers can supply a sparse frame directory with a truncated or crafted chunk file to crash applications or leak adjacent heap memory into decompressed output.

The CWILL (Formerly ParcelPanel) – Shipment Tracking, Tracking & Order Tracking for WooCommerce plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'data[].courier_code, data[].tracking_number (plus pp_sign for the auth bypass)' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 4.6.2 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. The authentication bypass is reachable only when the parcelpanel_api_key WordPress option is non-empty, which occurs automatically once an admin has opened or connected the ParcelPanel admin page; at that point any unauthenticated attacker can bypass the sole access gate by supplying a JSON boolean true as pp_sign, which PHP's loose == operator coerces to true when compared against the non-empty md5 hex string.
vp: cwill (formerly parcelpanel) – shipment tracking, tracking & order tracking for woocommerce

cves.d: The Hydrogen Calendar Embeds plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored DOM-Based Cross-Site Scripting via ICS Feed Event Fields (SUMMARY/DESCRIPTION/LOCATION) in all versions up to, and including, 3.0.3 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. This requires the attacker to have write access to an ICS feed that has been configured as a calendar source on the target WordPress site.

The My Calendar – Accessible Event Manager plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'mc_template (template body); event_title (payload storage)' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 3.8.13 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with subscriber-level access and above, to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. Successful exploitation requires the site to have granted mc_add_events to Subscriber-level users (a configurable plugin permission), and relies on a privileged user — such as an Administrator — following the event preview link surfaced on the My Calendar Events management screen.
Missing Authorization vulnerability in Kaliforms Kali Forms kali-forms allows Exploiting Incorrectly Configured Access Control Security Levels.This issue affects Kali Forms: from n/a through 2.4.32.

A use-after-free in Node.js HTTP/2 stream teardown can leak response memory, including the contents of other connections' response buffers, to a peer. When a stream is torn down while a write is still backpressured, for example by a peer `RST_STREAM` or by the server's own per-stream timeout destroying the stream, the stream's response buffer is freed but a reference to it is still used, so freed or unrelated heap memory is written to the socket instead of the intended response. On Node.js 26.x and 24.x the teardown can be driven purely by a remote peer once the window-size change from 26.9.0 and 24.22.0 is present, and on all supported lines the same defect is reachable through an application-initiated teardown such as a per-stream idle timeout. This vulnerability affects Node.js 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x.

The Recipe Card Blocks Lite plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to authorization bypass in all versions up to, and including, 4.0.1. This is due to the plugin not properly verifying that a user is authorized to perform an action. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with contributor-level access and above, to overwrite the stored post_content of any post or page on the site, including published posts and private drafts authored by administrators or other users.

A vulnerability has been found in hrshadhin CloudSchool up to 3.0.1. This affects the function EventController@store of the file app/Http/Controllers/Backend/EventController.php of the component Admin Content Management. Such manipulation of the argument data leads to cross site scripting. The attack can be launched remotely. The exploit has been disclosed to the public and may be used. The project was informed of the problem early through an issue report but has not responded yet.

In Splunk SOAR versions below 8.8.0, a user with edit permission for the container label of a pending external prompt could obtain the external prompt link through the Representational State Transfer (REST) API and use the link to view and resolve the associated approval.
The vulnerability is possible because the approval detail REST API includes the external prompt link in responses outside the assigned approval scope.
For more information see REST Approval (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/rest-api-reference/6.3.1/approval-endpoints/rest-approval), REST External Prompt (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/rest-api-reference/7.1.0/external-prompt-endpoints/rest-external-prompt), and Manage roles and permissions in Splunk SOAR (On-premises) (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-soar/soar-on-premises/administer-soar-on-premises/8.5.0/manage-your-splunk-soar-on-premises-users-and-accounts/manage-roles-and-permissions-in-splunk-soar-on-premises) in the Splunk documentation.

The Chatterbug Forms – Fast, Flexible WordPress Form Builder plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to arbitrary file deletion due to insufficient file path validation in the cbforms_delete_uploaded_files function in all versions up to, and including, 1.1 This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to delete arbitrary files on the server, which can easily lead to remote code execution when the right file is deleted (such as wp-config.php). Exploitation requires an administrator to delete the attacker-planted form entry, and the attacker must know or be able to guess the absolute path of a file writable by the PHP process. Successful exploitation additionally requires an action by an administrator — the attacker cannot trigger the vulnerability on their own.
vp: chatterbug forms – fast, flexible wordpress form builder

cves.d: A security flaw has been discovered in Gladys Assistant up to 4.71.0. This impacts an unknown function of the file server/lib/gateway/gateway.downloadBackup.js of the component Backup Restore Handler. The manipulation results in path traversal. The attack can be launched remotely. The exploit has been released to the public and may be used for attacks. Upgrading to version 4.72.0 will fix this issue. It is recommended to upgrade the affected component.

getID3 before 1.9.27 contains an XML external entity injection vulnerability in the XML2array helper function that fails to properly disable entity loading on PHP before 8.0. Attackers can craft malicious XML metadata in media files to disclose local files, perform server-side request forgery, or cause denial of service through entity expansion.

The urwid web display backend (urwid/display/web.py) generates web session identifiers (urwid_id) in Screen.start() by concatenating two random.randrange(10**9) calls that use Python's Mersenne Twister PRNG, which is not cryptographically secure. Each call consumes approximately 30 bits of PRNG state, and the Mersenne Twister internal state is approximately 19,937 bits, so an attacker who observes approximately 334 session IDs (for example via the X-Urwid-ID HTTP response header) can fully reconstruct the internal state and predict all past and future session IDs (Path B). The same identifier is also used as the filename of a FIFO created in the world-listable /tmp directory (for example /tmp/urwid375487765176907690.in), so any local user on the host can list /tmp to enumerate active session tokens directly (Path A). With a valid session ID, an attacker can read the victim's terminal screen via the polling endpoint, inject keystrokes into the victim's session (yielding OS-level code execution with the session owner's privileges if the session runs a shell), and inject exit sequences or flood the FIFO to terminate or crash the session. A prior Bandit S311 warning on this usage was suppressed with # noqa: S311 rather than fixed

Grav is a flat-file CMS. In Grav 1.7.0 before 1.7.53.3 and 2.0.0 before 2.0.22, when the debugger is enabled (system.debugger.enabled: true, which is not the default), the Clockwork profiler endpoint is exposed without authentication: InitializeProcessor::handleDebuggerRequest() intercepts any path containing /__clockwork/ during bootstrap and passes it to Debugger::debuggerRequest(), which performs no user lookup, IP restriction, or Clockwork authenticator check, and also supports anonymous pagination over the entire stored history. With the shipped censored: false default, each stored record contains raw request cookies (including Grav's session cookie, whose value is the PHP session id, allowing an attacker to resume another user's session, including an authenticated admin's), the full parsed request body (Grav's login form posts data[username]/data[password], so passwords are stored in plaintext because Clockwork's password filter only inspects top-level keys), and the site's entire system and plugin configuration, including operator-saved secrets such as SMTP credentials, third-party API keys, and licence keys. Authorization and X-API-Token headers are stored even when censored: true. On Grav 2.0, setting provider: debugbar does not avoid the issue because Grav forces the Clockwork provider for requests preferring a JSON response. The issue is fixed in 1.7.53.3 and 2.0.22, which restrict /__clockwork/ to server-local requests or requests presenting the new system.debugger.token secret and strip cookies and credential headers from stored records. Workarounds include setting debugger.enabled: false or blocking /__clockwork/ at the web server or CDN.

Nango through 0.72.6 fails to validate caller-supplied connection configuration values interpolated into provider token and proxy URL templates. Authenticated attackers can supply malicious configuration values to direct server requests at internal addresses or cloud metadata endpoints (0.71.3 and later block cloud metadata and loopback addresses by default but still permit private network addresses), potentially exfiltrating provider credentials.

knowns through 0.36.1 fails to properly validate template destination paths in the code generation template engine, allowing attackers to read and write arbitrary files outside the project root. Attackers can supply malicious templates that traverse directories to overwrite shell profiles, steal credentials, or achieve persistent code execution on victim systems.

Traefik is an HTTP reverse proxy and load balancer. In Traefik v1.x, v2.x through v2.11.55, and v3.0.0 through v3.7.11, header names are canonicalized only on dashes, so X-Auth-User, X_Auth_User and X.Auth.User are treated as three distinct headers by Traefik, while backends that derive variable names from header names (CGI, WSGI, PHP, NGINX and others) collapse them into a single variable. A client can therefore smuggle a dot-form alias of a header that Traefik manages past the middleware managing it — for example supplying X.Authenticated.User alongside the canonical X-Authenticated-User written by the ForwardAuth middleware — causing such a backend to read the client-supplied value instead of the identity Traefik asserted. In the tested configuration (PHP 8.2 built-in SAPI over an HTTP/1 backend path), Go's lexical header ordering makes the attacker-supplied value win deterministically, so a client that ForwardAuth admits as a low-privilege identity can be treated by the backend as a different user or role. Any header Traefik sets is affected, not only ForwardAuth's. This is an incomplete fix for GHSA-x677-9fxg-v5c5, which blocked only the underscore form. Fixed in v2.11.56 and v3.7.12, which add the aliasHeadersStrategy entry-point option; because it defaults to 'keep' for backwards compatibility, it must be explicitly set to 'delete' or 'reject' for the fix to take effect. Unmaintained release lines will not receive a patch.

Traefik is an HTTP reverse proxy and load balancer. In versions >= v2.8.2 through <= v2.11.55 and >= v3.0.0 through <= v3.7.11, the entryPoints.<name>.transport.respondingTimeouts settings — notably readTimeout, which is enabled by default at 60s — are not applied to the HTTP/3 request path. readTimeout is enforced as a deadline on the underlying TCP connection, which cannot be applied to a QUIC stream, and Traefik's HTTP/3 server is constructed without any timeout. As a result, on entry points with HTTP/3 enabled, an unauthenticated remote client that trickles request body bytes can hold a request open indefinitely and, with it, one upstream connection per request, exhausting bounded backend connection pools and causing denial of service.
